EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Trade Liberalization and Plant‐level Productivity in Chile, 1979-1986”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study specification.

Core idea: Plants that were in sectors (4-digit ISIC) experiencing large tariff cuts between 1979 and 1983 are the “treated,” while plants in sectors whose tariffs fell little (or only later) serve as the control. Because tariff cuts differed widely across sectors yet the timing was centrally set by the government, the policy provides plausibly exogenous cross-sectional variation interacted with a common time shock. A DID in plant-level panels (1979–1986) nets out:

• Plant fixed effects → time-invariant productivity differences  
• Year fixed effects → macro shocks (e.g., recession of 1982)  
• Sector-specific linear trends (optional) → slowly drifting technology

The event-study version traces pre- and post-effects and transparently tests the parallel-trend assumption.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable
TariffCut_s = (Tariff_s,1979 − Tariff_s,1983) / Tariff_s,1979  
Continuous measure ∈ [0,1]; larger values = larger liberalization.

Main treatment dummy
HighCut_s = 1{TariffCut_s ≥ median across sectors}. Robustness will use quartiles or the continuous interaction.

Control group
Plants in “LowCut” (below-median reductions). They serve as the counterfactual trend in the absence of large liberalization.

Treatment timing / event date
Policy announced in mid-1979, phased-in 1980–1983. We code 1979 as “pre,” 1980–1983 as transition, 1984–1986 as “post.” Our DID uses:

Post_t = 1{t ≥ 1984}

Event-study: d_k,t indicators for each year k relative to 1979.

(We purposely leave out the transition years in a robustness exercise to minimize anticipation/partial-treatment issues.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1 Parallel trends: In the absence of the tariff cuts, high-cut and low-cut sectors would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Before 1979 Chile’s tariffs had been stable for years, and no sector-specific shocks dominated 1976-78. Event-study pre-coefficients provide a direct test.

A2 No contemporaneous sector-specific confounders: Other policies (e.g., privatizations, subsidies) are not correlated with tariff-cut size.  
Plausibility: Trade reform was economy-wide and driven by macro goals, not sector lobbying (Edwards & Edwards, 1991).

A3 Stable composition of plants: Entry/exit cannot differentially bias the within-plant analysis.  
Plausibility: Exit is itself an outcome, but productivity regressions condition on surviving plants; we will supplement with inverse-probability weighting.

A4 No anticipation in outcomes prior to reform: Firms did not change behavior in 1978 merely on rumors.  
Plausibility: Reform details were unknown until mid-1979; pre-trend test covers 1976-78.

A5 SUTVA / no spillovers across sectors: A plant’s exposure is determined by its own sector’s tariff.  
Plausibility: Some input–output linkages exist; will check robustness by including weighted tariffs of input sectors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation

Threat 1: Demand shocks correlated with tariff cuts (e.g., export-boom sectors got large cuts).  
Fix: Control for baseline export share; include sector-year trends in robustness; instrument Δtariff with initial statutory rate (pre-1974 schedule) interacted with uniform reform percentage.

Threat 2: Differential survival bias (low-productivity plants exit more in high-cut sectors).  
Fix: (i) Model exit separately with a linear-probability DID; (ii) In productivity regressions, use Wooldridge (2007) selection correction or inverse-probability weighting predicted from pre-period characteristics.

Threat 3: Measurement error in tariffs at 4-digit level.  
Fix: Aggregate to 3-digit, instrument with average statutory rate in 1974, clustered s.e. at sector level; show results using import-penetration growth as alternative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline

```r
# 1. Load libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(did)        # for event-study (Callaway–Sant’Anna)
library(ggplot2)

# 2. Read and merge data
plants <- fread("chile_plants_1979_1986.csv")           # survey micro
tariffs <- fread("sector_tariffs_1974_1986.csv")        # 4-digit ISIC avg MFN
setkey(plants, sector4, year)
setkey(tariffs, sector4, year)
dat <- tariffs[plants]                                  # merge

# 3. Construct variables
dat[, TariffCut     := (tariff_1979 - tariff_1983)/tariff_1979, by = sector4]
median_cut <- median(unique(dat$TariffCut))
dat[, HighCut       := as.integer(TariffCut >= median_cut)]
dat[, Post84        := as.integer(year >= 1984)]
dat[, treat         := HighCut * Post84 ]               # DID interaction

# Outcomes
dat[, lnTFP  := log(tfp)]                               # tfp pre-computed in data
dat[, exited := 1 - alive]                              # indicate plant exit

# 4. Baseline DID: plant FE + year FE
did_mod <- feols(lnTFP ~ HighCut*Post84 | plant_id + year,
                 data = dat, cluster = "sector4")

summary(did_mod)

# 5. Event-study (absorbing plant & year FE)
dat[, rel_year := year - 1979]
# drop the transition years in base specification
ev_mod <- feols(lnTFP ~ i(rel_year, HighCut, ref = -1) | plant_id + year,
                data = dat, cluster = "sector4")
iplot(ev_mod)

# 6. Exit regression
exit_mod <- feols(exited ~ HighCut*Post84 | sector4 + year,
                  data = dat, family = "binomial", cluster = "sector4")

# 7. Robustness: Weight by inverse survival probability
# Estimate prob(survival) in pre-period
pre <- dat[year < 1979]
surv_mod <- glm(alive ~ lnTFP + size + capital_intensity,
                data = pre, family = binomial)
dat[, w_surv := 1/predict(surv_mod, newdata = dat, type = "response")]
did_w <- feols(lnTFP ~ HighCut*Post84 | plant_id + year,
               data = dat, weights = dat$w_surv, cluster = "sector4")
summary(did_w)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Theory (Melitz, 2003) predicts that tougher import competition:

• Forces the least-productive plants to exit.  
• Raises average productivity among survivors via reallocation and within-plant upgrading.

Hence:

• Coefficient on HighCut×Post should be positive for lnTFP (≈ 3–5 % on average).  
• Exit probability should rise by 2–4 pp in high-cut sectors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1 Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically supported ………………… 1  
C2 No other coincident sector policies ………………………………………… 0.5 (privatizations possible)  
C3 Stable composition / attrition addressed ………………………………… 0.5  
C4 No anticipation (pre-period flat) ………………………………………… 1  
C5 No interference between units ………………………………………… 0.5  

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 → “mostly credible but monitor threats.”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan sets up a transparent DID/event-study design using rich plant-level panel data and exploits cross-sector tariff heterogeneity to estimate the causal impact of Chile’s trade liberalization on productivity and exit.
